content: Rhinovirus, derived from the Greek word rhinmeaning nose, is a genus of viruses belonging to the Picornaviridae family. These viruses are the most common infectious agents in humans and are a primary cause of the common cold. There are over 105 serologic types of viruses that cause cold symptoms, with rhinoviruses accounting for approximately 50% of all cases. The viral genome is about 5 kilobases in length. At the 5′ end of the genome, there is a virus-encoded protein, and similar to mammalian mRNA, the genome contains a 3′ poly-A tail. Structural proteins are encoded in the 5′ region of the genome, while non-structural proteins are encoded at the 3′ end, a characteristic shared by all picornaviruses. The viral particles are non-enveloped and exhibit an icosahedral structure. Structure Rhinoviruses consist of a capsid that contains four viral proteins: VP1, VP2, VP3, and VP4. The major components of the protein capsid are VP1, VP2, and VP3, while the smaller VP4 protein has an extended structure and is located at the interface between the capsid and the RNA genome. Each of these proteins is present in 60 copies, forming an icosahedral assembly. Antibodies play a critical role in defending against rhinovirus infections, with epitopes located on the external regions of VP1, VP2, and VP3. Transmission and Epidemiology Rhinoviruses are transmitted through two primary routes: respiratory droplets in aerosols and contact with contaminated surfaces, including direct person-to-person contact. These viruses are found worldwide and are the leading cause of the common cold. Symptoms include sore throat, runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, and cough, often accompanied by muscle aches, fatigue, malaise, headache, muscle weakness, or loss of appetite. Fever and severe exhaustion are more characteristic of influenza rather than rhinovirus infections. Children may experience six to ten colds annually, with school-aged children potentially having up to twelve colds per year. In the United States, the incidence of colds is higher during the fall and winter months, with most infections occurring between September and April. This seasonality may be attributed to the start of the school year or increased indoor activity, which facilitates closer contact and viral transmission. Pathogenesis The primary entry point for rhinoviruses is the upper respiratory tract. The virus binds to ICAM-1 (intracellular adhesion molecule-1) receptors on respiratory epithelial cells. As the virus replicates and spreads, infected cells release distress signals in the form of chemokines and cytokines, which activate inflammatory mediators. Infection occurs rapidly, with the virus adhering to surface receptors within 15 minutes of entering the respiratory tract. The incubation period is typically 8–10 hours before symptoms manifest. Rhinoviruses rarely cause lower respiratory tract disease, likely due to their poor replication at the body temperature of 37°C. Novel Antiviral Drugs Intranasal administration of interferon-alpha has been shown to provide protection against rhinovirus infections. However, volunteers treated with this drug experienced side effects such as nasal bleeding, and resistance to the drug began to develop. Consequently, research on this drug was discontinued. Pleconaril, an orally bioavailable antiviral drug, is being developed for the treatment of picornavirus infections. This drug works by binding to a hydrophobic pocket in the VP1 protein, stabilizing the protein capsid to the extent that the virus cannot release its RNA genome into the target cell. Clinical trials in volunteers demonstrated that pleconaril significantly reduced mucus secretions and illness-associated symptoms. However, pleconaril is not currently available for the treatment of rhinoviral infections, as its efficacy is still under evaluation. Vaccine There are no vaccines available for rhinoviruses due to the lack of cross-protection between serotypes.
